strengths: Novel and well-motivated approach: Creates spatially consistent 3D adversarial objects with proper multi-view and temporal consistency, addressing a realistic non-contact attack scenario unlike prior texture or geometry-based methods

Technically sound methodology: The mesh placement strategy with location selection/distance constraints, occlusion-aware module using SAM, and BEV spatial feature-guided optimization (3-component loss) are well-designed and principled
Comprehensive ablation studies: Thorough investigation of shape initialization effects, distance robustness, and placement generalization provides good experimental rigor

Consistent and convincing results: Demonstrates vulnerabilities across three different BEV detectors (BEVDet, BEVDet4D, BEVFormer) with clear before/after comparisons, supporting the significance of findings

Strong visualizations and qualitative evidence: Figures 3-8 effectively demonstrate attack mechanisms in both image and BEV views, clearly showing suppressed vehicle predictions and induced false positives
Important safety implications: Addresses critical robustness concerns for autonomous driving systems in a practical adversarial setting
weaknesses: Limited baseline comparisons: Only compares against Adv3D; missing comparisons with other recent adversarial 3D detection attack methods, limiting positioning of the contribution
Narrow evaluation scope: Single dataset (nuScenes) and three models from 2021-2023 are insufficient for CVPR; no evaluation on KITTI, Waymo, or newer architectures

Significant acknowledged limitation undermines robustness claims: Attack effectiveness substantially degrades with distance (Tables 4, 9), and the paper admits poor generalization to different vehicle positions, limiting practical viability

Missing temporal consistency explanation: Despite claiming temporal consistency in the abstract, Section 3.3 does not clearly articulate how temporal consistency is enforced beyond multi-frame optimization

Practical feasibility not addressed: Limited discussion on how attackers would realistically place physical meshes in real-world scenarios; purely simulation-based evaluation with no sim-to-real analysis

Shallow analysis of vulnerability mechanisms: Paper demonstrates attacks succeed but provides limited insight into why BEV detectors fail (e.g., is it spatial reasoning, fusion design, or backbone architecture?)
No defense mechanisms or mitigation strategies: Paper is purely an attack paper without constructive contributions toward robustness solutions, limiting practical impact
Mixed transfer attack performance: Appendix B (Table 7) shows inconsistent transfer results (e.g., BEVDet→BEVFormer NDS: 0.3633→0.2073), raising questions about generalization

Reproducibility gaps: Missing implementation details (learning rates, optimizer, convergence criteria), no code availability mentioned, and unclear justification for design choices (e.g., 4 meshes per image limit)
No statistical validation: Results lack error bars or significance testing, and occlusion handling limited to SAM-based occlusions without handling scene object occlusions

strengths: Addresses important safety concern for BEV-based autonomous driving detectors
Well-motivated focus on spatial and temporal consistency across camera views and frames
Non-invasive approach to 3D adversarial attack is conceptually cleaner than texture-based modifications
Comprehensive experimental evaluation with extensive ablations (shape initialization, distance robustness, placement generalization)
Effective visualizations showing attack impact in both 2D image and 3D BEV space
Tests on multiple BEV detector architectures (BEVDet, BEVDet4D, BEVFormer)
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: standard combination of differentiable rendering and loss optimization (Eq. 7 uses conventional localization, adversarial, and confusion losses)
Narrow evaluation scope severely limits generalization claims: single dataset (nuScenes only), no KITTI/Waymo/other benchmarks, geographically limited
Modest empirical results: Attack Success Rates (0.657-0.715) contradict 'reliable suppression' claims; significant degradation with distance (ASR 0.391 at 3m) problematic for real autonomous driving
Key technical components lack clarity: BEV spatial feature guidance (Eq. 6) poorly explained, occlusion module using SAM is ad-hoc without justification/comparison
Incomplete ablations: no isolated analysis of occlusion-aware module, BEV feature guidance, or individual loss term contributions
Poor generalization characteristics: 47-point performance gap across shapes (cylinder 0.614 vs sphere 0.367); weak transfer across models (Table 7)
Insufficient baseline comparisons: only Adv3D compared despite mentioning many relevant methods ([15], [16], [18], [32], [37]); Adv3D comparison somewhat unfair (different problem formulation)

Reproducibility concerns: mesh topology unspecified, training time/compute not reported, specific hyperparameter values (α, β) not stated, code availability unmentioned, sensitivity to initialization unexplored
Limited scope of evaluation: fixed mesh placement relative to vehicle, only BEV detectors tested, no extreme weather/nighttime/severe occlusion scenarios
Misleading claims and framing: overclaimed effectiveness, Figure 1 comparison potentially misleading regarding 3D consistency/non-invasiveness of baselines

strengths: Novel problem formulation: Addresses practical, non-invasive 3D adversarial attacks that maintain spatial consistency across multiple camera views, more realistic than prior single-image approaches

Well-designed technical approach: Spatially consistent mesh representation via differentiable rendering, occlusion-aware module using SAM, and BEV spatial feature-guided optimization effectively target the model's perception space

Comprehensive experimental evaluation: Tests on three BEV architectures with extensive ablations on shape initialization, distance robustness, and placement generalization; includes transfer attack analysis and rich visualizations in both 2D and BEV views

Multiple evaluation metrics: Goes beyond Attack Success Rate to report mAP and NDS, providing nuanced assessment of performance impact; clear demonstration of transition from 'Init' to 'Adv' showing effectiveness
Detailed reproducibility information: Specifies mesh topologies, hyperparameters, training procedures, dataset details, and architectural choices; enables reasonable reproduction efforts
Honest limitations discussion: Section 4.5 transparently acknowledges method constraints including poor random placement performance and micro-rendering inconsistencies
weaknesses: Limited baseline comparisons: Only compares with Adv3D [17]; missing comparisons with other recent non-invasive 3D adversarial methods, geometry-based approaches, and simpler baselines

Questionable practical realism: Assumes perfect camera calibration, ideal lighting, flawless differentiable rendering, and known camera parameters—unrealistic in adversarial scenarios; no evaluation against simple defenses (adversarial training, input denoising)

Significant generalization limitations: Only evaluated on nuScenes; transfer attacks show substantial performance drops (e.g., 0.2819→0.1775 mAP); unclear how methods generalize to other datasets or scale to multiple adversarial objects

Insufficient attack mechanism analysis: Limited investigation into which specific BEV features are exploited; missing feature visualizations or saliency analysis; design choices (shape selection, loss weightings) lack thorough justification
Evaluation gaps on temporal consistency: Despite testing BEVDet4D, temporal robustness across frames is not thoroughly evaluated; single-frame attacks limit assessment of temporal detectors

Practical threat model concerns: Real sensors introduce noise, compression, and artifacts not modeled; requires perfect rendering and precise camera parameters; no real-world validation or realistic sensor simulation

Somewhat incremental technical novelty: Differentiable rendering for adversarial attacks and BEV feature optimization are established techniques; individual components are sound but not particularly novel

strengths: Novel problem formulation of spatially consistent, non-invasive 3D adversarial objects that is more practical than prior invasive approaches requiring direct target modification
Technically sound approach combining differentiable rendering for 3D consistency with realistic occlusion processing to ensure physical plausibility
Comprehensive experimental evaluation including extensive ablations, tests on three state-of-the-art detectors, and both digital and physical validation experiments
Substantial empirical improvements over baselines (AdV3D and UAP) with 30-40% ASR gains in multiple scenarios
Physical attack validation through 3D-printed mesh experiments demonstrates transfer from digital to real-world domain
Good reproducibility with detailed implementation information in supplementary material
weaknesses: Limited scope restricted to camera-based BEV detectors only; title claims universality but doesn't evaluate LiDAR-based, fusion approaches, or other 3D detection frameworks
Insufficient cross-dataset and cross-detector generalization analysis; primarily evaluated on nuScenes with no systematic transfer learning evaluation across datasets or detector architectures
No discussion of defense mechanisms or evaluation against adversarial training/certified defenses, limiting practical robustness insights
Method requires strong assumptions (perfect 3D scene geometry, camera calibration, detector architecture knowledge) with limited analysis of applicability in dynamic real-world scenarios
Object sizes and placement ranges are relatively constrained (small cylinders/cubes, 0-7.27m distances); scalability to diverse object geometries unexplored
Physical validation limited to controlled outdoor settings with fixed cameras; doesn't replicate dynamic driving scenarios with moving vehicles and changing lighting conditions

Technical presentation issues including some ad-hoc design choices (e.g., sign choices in distance calculations in Sec. 3.2) and hand-crafted feature-guided optimization that lacks principled justification
Limited evaluation metrics (primarily ASR) with no computational cost analysis, robustness quantification, or real-time deployment feasibility assessment
Comparison restricted to two invasive baselines; missing comparison with other potential non-invasive methods or random placement oracles

strengths: Addresses practical problem of multi-view consistent adversarial 3D objects for BEV detectors with good motivation for non-invasive attacks
Comprehensive technical pipeline integrating differentiable rendering, realistic occlusion processing, and feature-guided optimization with thoughtful design choices
Extensive experimental evaluation across multiple detectors (BEVDet, BEVDet4D, BEVFormer) with thorough ablation studies on shape initialization, distance robustness, and loss components
Demonstrates significant empirical results with ~41% performance degradation and attempts physical validation through printed mesh experiments
Well-documented supplementary material with detailed implementation specifics for reproducibility
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: pipeline primarily combines existing techniques (differentiable rendering, feature guidance, occlusion modeling) without fundamental innovation or significant algorithmic contribution

Critical experimental gaps undermine generalization claims: evaluation on single dataset only (nuScenes), no LiDAR-based detector testing despite their importance in autonomous driving, sparse baseline comparisons (primarily AdV3D from 2015)

Questionable physical plausibility despite claims: adversarial meshes (cubes, spheres) appear visually artificial and easily detectable by humans or safety systems; Fig. 6 clearly shows unnatural object appearance; controlled physical validation doesn't reflect real driving scenarios

Significant generalization limitations: cross-model transfer shows substantial performance drops (mAP drops from 0.3086 to 0.2835/0.2514), robustness severely degrades with distance (Table 5: ASR from 0.66 at 0.1m to 0.20 at 1.0m), 'universal' framing overclaimed

Incomplete technical justification: fixed loss weights (α, β = 10) lack sensitivity analysis, scene confusion loss (Eq. 8) appears ad-hoc, no principled explanation for BEV feature guidance vs. alternatives, Table 7 ablation shows marginal improvements
Missing critical analysis: no defense mechanisms or attack detection discussion, no failure case analysis, no user studies on human perception, incomplete treatment of physical plausibility concerns
Methodological limitations: requires known camera intrinsics and scene geometry, training on only 4 meshes seems limited, mesh initialization strategy is scene-specific with no sensitivity analysis
Reproducibility concerns: no code release mentioned despite supplementary material, hyperparameter choices lack justification, unclear feature map extraction details

Overclaiming of contributions: 'first framework' and 'universal' claims not well-supported given detector-specific optimization and documented limitations; AdV3D comparison uses different experimental protocols

strengths: Novel contribution: First non-invasive, 3D-consistent universal adversarial object framework for BEV detectors, addressing an important security gap in autonomous driving systems
Comprehensive methodology combining automatic mesh placement, differentiable rendering for multi-view consistency, realistic occlusion handling, and BEV feature-guided optimization
Extensive experimental validation across three BEV detectors with thorough ablation studies demonstrating necessity of each component
Both digital and physical validation: Proof-of-concept physical attack experiment (Section 4.5) strengthens credibility and demonstrates real-world transferability
Robust evaluation across multiple dimensions: varying distances, object shapes, viewpoints, and scene configurations
Clear mathematical formulation and well-motivated technical design choices
Important insights into vulnerabilities of BEV-based detection systems and their over-reliance on learned environmental priors
Comprehensive supplementary material with extensive implementation details, additional ablations, and extended analysis
Well-presented paper with effective visualizations and clear exposition of methodology
weaknesses: Limited scope of detector models: Only three BEV detectors tested from similar architectural families; lacks evaluation on diverse architectures or other detection paradigms (LiDAR-based, fusion methods)
Single dataset evaluation: Testing only on nuScenes limits generalizability claims; validation on KITTI, Waymo, or other datasets would strengthen findings
Limited physical validation: Only one physical attack scenario demonstrated in controlled conditions; lacks evaluation across different weather, lighting, and real-world traffic complexity
Insufficient defense analysis: No discussion of mitigation strategies or evaluation against adversarial training/hardening techniques; missed opportunity to propose defensive mechanisms
Incomplete comparative analysis: Limited baselines (mainly Adv3D); comparison with broader adversarial attack literature and recent 3D object attack methods lacking
Missing computational analysis: No discussion of optimization time, computational requirements, or scalability; cost comparison with baselines not provided
Limited object category breakdown: Insufficient analysis of which detection classes (car, truck, pedestrian) are most vulnerable; class-specific vulnerability analysis would provide deeper insights
Generalization analysis incomplete: Impact of model updates, adversarial retraining, and attack longevity not explored; transfer dynamics across distant model families insufficiently analyzed
Physical-to-digital gap not systematically characterized: Uncertainty about practical deployment viability across varied real-world conditions
